notice: RN bank batch 68: Management of Care and Safety: priorities, assignment, legal practice, referrals and triage. Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026. See REVIEW-LOG.md.

questions.stem: After receiving the 0700 handoff on a medical-surgical unit, the nurse reviews four assigned clients. Which client should the nurse see first?

options.text: A client 2 days after a colectomy who rates incisional pain 7 of 10; the last IV morphine dose was 3 hours ago and the heart rate is 98/min
A client with COPD whose SpO2 is 89% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula, respiratory rate 22/min, with a documented baseline SpO2 of 88% to 92%
A client 1 day after a hip replacement who reports new sharp chest pain on inspiration and is restless, heart rate 118/min
A client with type 1 diabetes whose 0700 fingerstick glucose is 64 mg/dL, who is alert and is due a breakfast tray in 30 minutes

rationale.correct: Use the ABCs and expected versus unexpected findings: an acute change suggesting pulmonary embolism outranks pain, a known chronic baseline and mild hypoglycemia in an alert client.

perOption.a: Pain needs prompt treatment, and the heart rate fits pain; this client is stable enough to be seen second.
perOption.b: These values are within this client's known baseline, so they are expected for the disease.
perOption.c: Sudden pleuritic chest pain, restlessness and tachycardia after hip surgery suggest a pulmonary embolism, which is life-threatening.
perOption.d: Mild hypoglycemia in an alert client is treated quickly with 15 g of oral carbohydrate, which the nurse can delegate or do right after seeing the unstable client.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose the client with an unexpected, life-threatening change first.

questions.stem: The RN is working with an assistive personnel (AP) on a surgical unit. Which task is most appropriate for the RN to delegate to the AP?

options.text: Feeding lunch to a client after a stroke whose bedside swallow screen was completed by speech therapy an hour ago
Walking in the hall with a client 2 days after a knee replacement who has walked twice today with physical therapy using a walker
Taking the vital signs of a client who returned from a cardiac catheterization through the femoral artery 15 minutes ago
Reinforcing the teaching about incentive spirometer use for a client who is refusing to use it because of pain

rationale.correct: Delegate tasks with predictable outcomes for stable clients that need no assessment, teaching or judgment.

perOption.a: The first meal after a swallow evaluation needs the nurse's judgment to watch for aspiration; the client's response is not yet predictable.
perOption.b: The client's response is established and predictable, and ambulation with a known device is within the AP's training.
perOption.c: Vital signs early after a procedure are part of the nurse's assessment for bleeding and instability; the client is not yet stable.
perOption.d: Teaching and addressing barriers such as pain need nursing judgment and cannot be delegated to AP.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Delegate safely to assistive personnel.

questions.stem: Tonight a 24-bed medical unit is staffed with two RNs and one licensed practical nurse (LPN). Of the four clients below, which one should the charge nurse give to the LPN?

options.text: A client admitted 20 minutes ago with chest pain radiating to the jaw whose first troponin result is still pending
A client with type 2 diabetes who needs scheduled subcutaneous insulin and a dressing change on a chronic venous ulcer
A client who is about to start a first unit of packed red blood cells for a hemoglobin of 6.9 g/dL
A client 4 hours after a thyroidectomy who reports a tingling feeling around the mouth and is hoarse

rationale.correct: Assign the LPN stable clients with predictable outcomes; keep new admissions, transfusions and clients with changing findings for the RN.

perOption.a: A new admission with possible acute coronary syndrome needs the RN's initial assessment and is unstable.
perOption.b: This client is stable, with predictable care that falls within the LPN's scope: giving subcutaneous insulin and doing sterile or clean dressing changes.
perOption.c: Monitoring during the first 15 minutes of a transfusion needs RN assessment for reactions.
perOption.d: Perioral tingling can signal hypocalcemia after thyroid surgery, and this client needs RN assessment now.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Assign clients within the LPN's scope.

questions.stem: A nurse from the pediatric unit is floated to an adult medical-surgical unit for the shift. Which 2 clients should the charge nurse assign to the float nurse?

options.text: A 34-year-old client on day 3 of IV antibiotics for cellulitis of the leg who is afebrile and walking independently
A 52-year-old client receiving a continuous heparin infusion whose next aPTT is due in 1 hour and may need a dose change
A 29-year-old client with asthma who is being discharged later today after teaching about inhaler technique
A 70-year-old client who is newly admitted from the emergency department with acute delirium and a possible urinary tract infection
A 61-year-old client 6 hours after a bowel resection with a nasogastric tube and a patient-controlled analgesia pump

rationale.correct: Assign float staff the stable clients whose care is closest to their usual practice, and keep unstable or unit-specific care with the regular staff.

perOption.a: Stable, with routine care any nurse can provide; IV antibiotics and wound checks are familiar to a pediatric nurse.
perOption.b: Adjusting a weight-based heparin protocol for an adult is unit-specific care better kept for a regular staff nurse.
perOption.c: Stable, and asthma care and inhaler teaching are familiar to a pediatric nurse.
perOption.d: An unstable new admission needs a nurse experienced with older adults and the unit's admission routines.
perOption.e: Early postoperative adult care with a PCA needs frequent specialized assessment and is better kept for unit staff.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Assign float staff appropriately.

questions.stem: The RN, an LPN and an assistive personnel (AP) are caring for clients on a medical unit. For each task, indicate the team member who is the most appropriate to perform it.

rows.text: Admission assessment of a client with pneumonia
Reinforcing insulin pen teaching the RN gave yesterday
Evaluating the response to a first dose of IV furosemide
Giving scheduled oral metoprolol to a stable client

rationale.correct: The RN keeps assessment, initial teaching and evaluation; LPNs give medications and reinforce teaching for stable clients; AP do routine tasks with set steps.

perOption.r1:c1: The initial assessment is the RN's responsibility and cannot be delegated.
perOption.r1:c2: LPNs collect data but do not complete the initial admission assessment.
perOption.r2:c1: The RN could do this, but reinforcing established teaching is within LPN scope, which frees the RN.
perOption.r2:c2: LPNs may reinforce teaching the RN has already given.
perOption.r2:c3: AP do not teach clients about medications.
perOption.r3:c1: The RN could do this, but it is a routine task suited to AP.
perOption.r3:c2: The LPN could do this, but it does not need a licensed nurse.
perOption.r3:c3: Specimen collection with standard steps is within AP training.
perOption.r4:c1: Evaluating a new treatment's effect needs RN judgment.
perOption.r4:c2: Evaluating a first response to a new therapy is not within LPN scope.
perOption.r4:c3: AP can report urine output but cannot evaluate a drug's effect.
perOption.r5:c1: The RN could do this, but oral medications for a stable client are within LPN scope.
perOption.r5:c2: LPNs give oral medications to stable clients.
perOption.r5:c3: AP do not give medications in acute care.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Match tasks to each team member's scope.

questions.stem: The nurse is asked to witness a client's signature on the consent form for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy scheduled in 1 hour. Which actions are appropriate for the nurse? Select all that apply.

options.text: Confirm that the client is signing the form of their own free will
Explain the risks of the surgery when the client asks what could go wrong
Check whether the client received an opioid or sedative in the last few hours before signing
Notify the surgeon when the client says they do not understand what will be removed
Ask the client's spouse to sign instead because the client seems anxious
Witness the signature after the client signs it alone in the room while the nurse is away

rationale.correct: The nurse witnesses a voluntary signature by a competent, informed client and calls the surgeon when the client has questions or doubts.

perOption.a: Witnessing includes confirming the consent is voluntary.
perOption.b: Explaining risks, benefits and alternatives is the surgeon's duty; the nurse notifies the surgeon about the question.
perOption.c: A client under the effect of sedating drugs may not be able to give informed consent.
perOption.d: Lack of understanding means consent is not informed; the surgeon must explain again before the client signs.
perOption.e: An anxious adult with capacity still gives their own consent; anxiety does not transfer the decision to the spouse.
perOption.f: The witness must see the client sign the form.

questions.educationalObjective: Describe the nurse's role in informed consent.

questions.stem: A client who is a Jehovah's Witness has a hemoglobin of 6.8 g/dL after a gastrointestinal bleed. The client is alert and oriented, understands the risks and refuses a blood transfusion. The client's spouse tells the nurse, "Give the blood anyway. I'll take responsibility." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "I can ask the provider to talk with you both again, because your consent can override the refusal in an emergency."
"Your spouse can make this decision. I will tell the provider so we can discuss treatments that do not use blood."
"I will ask the ethics committee to decide whether we can give the blood, since the bleeding is serious."
"We will wait and give the blood if the client loses consciousness, because then consent is implied."

rationale.correct: An adult with capacity has the right to refuse treatment, even life-saving treatment. The nurse supports the decision and works with the provider on acceptable alternatives.

perOption.a: A spouse's consent cannot override the refusal of an adult who has decision-making capacity.
perOption.b: A competent adult may refuse treatment; the nurse respects the decision and advocates for alternatives such as iron, erythropoietin or volume expanders.
perOption.c: An ethics consult can support staff, but it does not decide for a competent adult who has clearly refused.
perOption.d: Implied emergency consent does not apply when the client has already made a known, informed refusal.

questions.educationalObjective: Advocate for a competent client's refusal of treatment.

questions.stem: A client with a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order and metastatic lung cancer becomes diaphoretic and shaky, and the fingerstick glucose is 48 mg/dL. A new graduate nurse asks whether the prescribed IV dextrose should be given because of the DNR order. What should the nurse tell the new graduate?

options.text: "Ask the provider for a new order first, since a DNR means comfort care only."
"Give the dextrose. The DNR order applies to CPR if the heart or breathing stops."
"Check with the family first, because the client's wishes about treatment may have changed."
"Offer oral juice only, because IV treatment would go against the DNR order."

rationale.correct: DNR means no CPR. Unless other treatments are specifically limited, the client receives all other prescribed care.

perOption.a: A DNR order is not a comfort-care-only order; prescribed treatments continue unless they are also withdrawn.
perOption.b: A DNR order limits resuscitation only; it does not withhold other treatment such as correcting hypoglycemia.
perOption.c: The client's current orders guide care; delaying treatment of hypoglycemia to call the family is unsafe.
perOption.d: IV dextrose is not resuscitation, and a shaky, diaphoretic client may not swallow safely.

questions.educationalObjective: Interpret the scope of a DNR order.

questions.stem: A caller says she is the daughter of a client who had a breast biopsy yesterday and asks the nurse for the results. The client's record lists the daughter as someone who may receive information and gives a privacy code. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the results, since the daughter is listed in the record and correctly states the client's birth date
Ask the caller for the privacy code, then share general condition and refer results to the provider
Tell the caller that no information can be given by telephone under any circumstances
Transfer the call to the client's room so the client can decide what to share

rationale.correct: Confirm a caller's identity with the agreed code before sharing anything, and leave new diagnostic results to the provider.

perOption.a: The caller's identity is not yet confirmed, and the provider shares new biopsy results first.
perOption.b: Verifying the code protects confidentiality, and the provider discusses new results with the client first.
perOption.c: Information can be shared by phone with an authorized person once identity is confirmed.
perOption.d: This is reasonable only after the client agrees; it does not address verifying who is calling.

questions.educationalObjective: Protect confidential information over the telephone.

questions.stem: At 0730 the nurse notices that a colleague has slurred speech, smells of alcohol and is drawing up an IV opioid for a client. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Talk with the colleague privately after the shift and suggest the employee assistance program
Report the colleague to the state board of nursing before the shift ends
Stop the colleague from giving the drug and notify the charge nurse right away
Ask the colleague whether they feel well and stay at the bedside to watch closely while they give the dose

rationale.correct: Suspected impairment is a client safety issue: remove the nurse from care now and notify the immediate supervisor, who follows the facility's process.

perOption.a: Waiting leaves clients at risk from an impaired nurse for the whole shift.
perOption.b: Reporting may be needed later, but it does not protect the client who is about to receive the drug.
perOption.c: Client safety comes first: the impaired nurse must be removed from care immediately and the supervisor notified.
perOption.d: Watching does not prevent harm; an impaired nurse should not give any medication.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a colleague's impaired practice.

questions.stem: A client with pneumonia who is receiving IV antibiotics and has decision-making capacity says, "I'm going home now. I have a business to run." The client starts to get dressed. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the client that they cannot leave until the provider has seen them
Notify the provider and explain the risks of leaving before treatment ends
Remove the IV catheter at once and give the client the discharge papers
Call security to stay with the client until the provider arrives on the unit

rationale.correct: A competent client may leave against medical advice. Inform the provider, explain the risks, ask the client to sign the AMA form and document; do not restrain.

perOption.a: Keeping a competent client against their will can be false imprisonment.
perOption.b: The client has the right to leave; the nurse informs the provider and ensures the client understands the risks so the decision is informed.
perOption.c: Removing the IV is needed before the client leaves, but discharge papers and teaching come after the provider is informed.
perOption.d: Security cannot hold a competent adult who wants to leave.

Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.educationalObjective: Manage a client leaving against medical advice.

questions.stem: A client was found on the floor beside the bed. The client denies pain, and the nurse's assessment finds no injury. Which entry should the nurse make in the client's health record?

options.text: "Client found on floor beside bed at 0215. Denies hitting head. No injury found. Provider notified."
"Client fell out of bed at 0215 because the bed alarm was off. Incident report filed."
"Client found on floor at 0215, probably fell while trying to go to the bathroom alone."
"Client on floor at 0215. AP had not answered the call light. Charge nurse aware."

rationale.correct: Chart only facts, care given and notifications. The incident report is a separate quality document and is not mentioned in the record.

perOption.a: Objective, factual and complete; it records what was seen and done.
perOption.b: It states a cause the nurse did not see and mentions the incident report, which does not belong in the record.
perOption.c: "Probably" is speculation; the record should hold facts only.
perOption.d: Blaming staff in the record is inappropriate; quality concerns go in the incident report.

questions.educationalObjective: Document an unusual occurrence.

questions.stem: The nurse discovers that a client received 10 units of insulin lispro instead of the prescribed 4 units 10 minutes ago. Place the nurse's actions in the order they should be done.

items.text: Complete an incident report as the facility requires
Carry out prescribed treatment and recheck the glucose often
Check the client's level of consciousness and fingerstick glucose
Notify the provider of the error and the assessment findings

rationale.correct: After an error: assess the client, notify the provider, treat and monitor, then report through the quality system.

perOption.a: The client's safety comes first: assess for hypoglycemia.
perOption.b: The provider needs the facts to prescribe treatment.
perOption.c: Monitoring continues while the extra insulin peaks.
perOption.d: Reporting supports quality improvement once the client is safe.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a medication error in order.

questions.stem: Two assistive personnel are arguing loudly in the hallway, in front of clients and visitors, about who should care for a client with a heavy workload. What should the charge nurse do first?

options.text: Ask both staff members to continue the conversation in a private room
Divide the client's care between both staff members for the rest of the shift
Ask each staff member to write a statement about the disagreement for the manager
Tell both staff members to settle the problem themselves during their break

rationale.correct: Address conflict promptly and privately, then help the people involved reach a solution.

perOption.a: Moving the conflict away from clients protects their privacy and dignity and lets the charge nurse listen to both sides.
perOption.b: This may help later, but it does not stop the public argument.
perOption.c: Written statements may follow, but the first need is to stop the public conflict.
perOption.d: Delaying lets the argument continue in front of clients.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Manage staff conflict.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old client with heart failure has been readmitted for the third time in 30 days with fluid overload. The client lives alone and tells the nurse, "I take my water pill every other day so the bottle lasts until my check comes." Which referral should the nurse request first?

options.text: A dietitian, to review sodium and fluid limits with the client before discharge
A home health nurse, to visit after discharge and check weight and lung sounds
A social worker or case manager, to find help paying for the client's medications
A pharmacist, to explain how furosemide works and why every dose matters

rationale.correct: Find the cause of nonadherence before choosing a referral. Cost problems go to social work or case management.

perOption.a: Diet matters in heart failure, but the client's own words point to a financial barrier to taking the medication.
perOption.b: Home monitoring is useful, but it does not solve the client's inability to pay for medication.
perOption.c: The readmissions come from skipping furosemide to save money; financial resources address the cause.
perOption.d: The client is skipping doses because of cost, not lack of knowledge.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Refer a client to resources for medication costs.

questions.stem: A client is 3 days after an ischemic stroke. The nurse notes the client coughs when drinking thin liquids, has trouble buttoning a shirt with the right hand and walks with an unsteady gait. Which referral is the priority?

options.text: Occupational therapy, to help the client relearn dressing and other daily activities
Physical therapy, to assess gait and provide an assistive device for walking
Speech-language pathology, to evaluate swallowing and recommend a safe diet
A dietitian, to calculate calorie needs and choose foods the client prefers

rationale.correct: Use the ABCs to rank referrals: aspiration risk (airway) comes before mobility and self-care.

perOption.a: Fine-motor and self-care training is important but is not the most urgent need.
perOption.b: Gait training lowers fall risk, but aspiration is a more immediate threat.
perOption.c: Coughing with thin liquids suggests dysphagia and aspiration risk, which threatens the airway.
perOption.d: A dietitian helps with nutrition after the safe diet texture is known.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize referrals after a stroke.

questions.stem: The nurse is planning discharge for three clients. For each situation, choose the most appropriate referral.

cells.text: New colostomy; has trouble fitting the pouch and has red, weeping skin around the stoma
New spinal cord injury; needs a wheelchair, a ramp and a shower chair at home
New type 2 diabetes; works night shifts and asks how to plan meals

options.text: Wound, ostomy and continence nurse
Physical therapist
Dietitian
Dietitian
Occupational therapist
Speech-language pathologist
Wound, ostomy and continence nurse
Speech-language pathologist
Dietitian

rationale.correct: Match each need to the discipline that addresses it: ostomy nurse for pouching and skin, OT for adaptive equipment, dietitian for meal planning.

perOption.b1:a: Peristomal skin damage and pouch fitting are specialist ostomy care.
perOption.b1:b: PT addresses mobility, not pouching or skin care.
perOption.b1:c: Diet may matter later, but the skin problem needs ostomy expertise first.
perOption.b2:a: Nutrition is not the issue described.
perOption.b2:b: OT assesses the home and recommends adaptive equipment for daily living.
perOption.b2:c: No speech or swallowing problem is described.
perOption.b3:a: There is no wound or ostomy.
perOption.b3:b: SLP does not plan diets for diabetes.
perOption.b3:c: A dietitian builds a meal plan around the client's work schedule and glucose goals.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Choose discharge referrals.

questions.stem: At 1800 the nurse realizes that the 1400 dose of oral levetiracetam given to a client was never documented in the electronic health record. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Document the dose now as a late entry, giving the time it was actually given
Change the system clock setting so the entry appears at 1400
Ask the next nurse to document the dose during the night shift
Leave the dose undocumented, since the next dose is due at 2200 anyway

rationale.correct: Document late entries promptly, labeled as late, with the real times, and never alter or omit entries.

perOption.a: A late entry, clearly labeled with the current time and the time the drug was given, keeps the record accurate.
perOption.b: Altering times falsifies the record.
perOption.c: Nurses document only care they gave themselves.
perOption.d: An undocumented dose could lead to a double dose and leaves the record incomplete.

questions.educationalObjective: Make a late entry in the health record.

questions.stem: The nurse receives this handoff report at 1900. Highlight the findings the nurse should follow up first.

segments.text: Room 12 is a 66-year-old client on day 2 after a right total knee replacement.
Pain is 4 of 10 after oxycodone at 1600
Urine output has been 90 mL since 1100
The client walked to the chair twice with physical therapy
The client's heart rate went from 82 to 108/min over the afternoon
The dressing has a 2 cm spot of dry drainage
. The client is on enoxaparin 40 mg daily.

rationale.correct: Low urine output and rising heart rate after joint surgery are unexpected and can signal bleeding or hypovolemia; they need assessment first.

perOption.s2: Pain is controlled; reassess at the next scheduled time.
perOption.s4: Less than 30 mL/hr suggests low perfusion or retention and needs follow-up now.
perOption.s8: A rising heart rate can signal bleeding, infection or a pulmonary embolism.
perOption.s10: A small dry spot is expected; mark it and monitor.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize priority findings in a handoff report.

questions.stem: A client who speaks Vietnamese and little English is to be taught about a new anticoagulant before discharge. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Arrange a certified medical interpreter for the teaching session
Ask the client's 12-year-old grandchild, who is visiting, to interpret
Look at and speak directly to the client rather than the interpreter
Use the teach-back method to confirm the client understands
Give printed instructions in English to read at home
Allow extra time, because interpreted sessions take longer

rationale.correct: Use a qualified interpreter, speak to the client, confirm understanding with teach-back and give materials in the client's language.

perOption.a: Trained interpreters give accurate meaning and protect confidentiality.
perOption.b: Family members, especially children, may leave things out or change the meaning.
perOption.c: Speaking to the client respects them and keeps the conversation focused on them.
perOption.d: Teach-back checks understanding of key safety points such as bleeding signs.
perOption.e: Written material should be in the client's preferred language.
perOption.f: Rushing an interpreted session leads to gaps in understanding.

questions.educationalObjective: Advocate for a client with limited English proficiency.

questions.stem: During a mass casualty incident, the nurse uses START triage. Which victim should the nurse tag as immediate (red)?

options.text: An adult walking around the scene holding an arm with an open forearm fracture
An adult who does not breathe even after the nurse repositions the airway
An adult with a respiratory rate of 34/min who follows simple commands
An adult with a thigh deformity, respiratory rate 20/min, radial pulse present, who follows commands

rationale.correct: START triage: walking is green; not breathing after airway positioning is black; respirations above 30, absent radial pulse or delayed capillary refill, or inability to follow commands is red; everyone else is yellow.

perOption.a: A victim who can walk is tagged minor (green) at first, even with a painful injury.
perOption.b: No breathing after the airway is opened is tagged expectant or deceased (black) in START.
perOption.c: A respiratory rate above 30/min meets the START criteria for immediate care.
perOption.d: Normal breathing, perfusion and mental status with an inability to walk make this victim delayed (yellow).

questions.educationalObjective: Triage victims with START.

questions.stem: A client who pulled out a nasogastric tube is in soft wrist restraints under a current provider order. The nurse checks the restraints. Which finding requires the nurse to act right away?

options.text: Two fingers slide easily under each wrist restraint
The restraint straps are tied to the movable side rails
The restraints are fastened with quick-release knots
The order was written 6 hours ago and renewed by the provider

rationale.correct: Secure restraints to the bed frame with quick-release knots, check two-finger fit and circulation, and keep a current order.

perOption.a: This shows the restraints are snug but not too tight.
perOption.b: Straps tied to side rails can tighten or injure the client when the rails are moved; they must be tied to the bed frame.
perOption.c: Quick-release knots are correct, so the restraints can be removed fast in an emergency.
perOption.d: A current, renewed order is required and is present.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.educationalObjective: Check restraint safety.

questions.stem: A client who weighs 112 kg (247 lb) and cannot bear weight on either leg after a spinal cord injury needs to move from the bed to a wheelchair. How should the nurse plan the transfer?

options.text: Use a full-body mechanical lift with a second staff member
Use a gait belt and a two-person stand-and-pivot transfer to the chair
Ask three staff members to lift the client together using the draw sheet
Place a slide board and have the client move across it independently

rationale.correct: Clients who cannot bear weight are moved with mechanical lift equipment and enough staff, not by manual lifting.

perOption.a: Safe handling guidelines call for a mechanical lift when a client cannot bear weight; it protects both the client and staff.
perOption.b: A stand-and-pivot needs the client to bear some weight, which this client cannot do.
perOption.c: Manual lifting of a heavy, non-weight-bearing client injures staff and is not safe practice.
perOption.d: A slide board needs good upper-body strength and balance, which are not described here.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: An 82-year-old client started oxycodone for back pain and takes furosemide each morning. The client got up alone to go to the bathroom last night and was found dizzy beside the bed. Which actions should the nurse include in the fall prevention plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the bed in the lowest position with the wheels locked
Raise all four side rails at night so the client stays in bed
Offer help to the bathroom on a schedule, including before sleep
Give a sleeping pill at bedtime so the client sleeps through the night
Close the room door at night to reduce noise from the hallway

rationale.correct: Low and locked beds, and scheduled toileting address this client's risks; extra rails, sedation and less observation increase them.

perOption.a: A low, locked bed reduces injury if the client falls or gets up alone.
perOption.b: Four raised rails are a restraint and increase falls when clients climb over them.
perOption.c: Scheduled toileting reduces unplanned trips to the bathroom, a common cause of night falls.
perOption.d: Sedatives add to opioid sedation and increase fall risk.
perOption.e: A closed door reduces staff observation of a high-risk client.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: After a regional disaster, the hospital activates its emergency plan and asks each unit to identify clients who can be discharged early to free beds. Which client is the best candidate for early discharge?

options.text: A client 1 day after a myocardial infarction whose chest pain has resolved
A client with a deep vein thrombosis whose aPTT on heparin is still below the therapeutic range
A client 3 days after an appendectomy who is eating a regular diet and walking in the hall
A client newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes who has not yet given an insulin injection

rationale.correct: In a surge, discharge the most stable clients with predictable recovery who can safely continue care at home.

perOption.a: Clients are at highest risk of dysrhythmias in the first days after an MI and need monitoring.
perOption.b: Anticoagulation is not yet therapeutic, so the client needs continued hospital care.
perOption.c: The client is recovering as expected and could safely finish recovery at home.
perOption.d: Discharge before the client can manage insulin safely would put the client at risk.
